transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Well, I guess I'm here because I just can't shake this feeling that work isn't safe anymore. Which is strange to say out loud because I'm a computer systems analyst, mostly just sitting at a desk. Actually, they just replaced all our monitors last week with these huge ultrawide screens. They're supposed to be better for looking at multiple server logs at once, but honestly, it just takes up my whole desk and I had to move my favorite coffee mug to a filing cabinet. It's the mug my parents got me when I finished my master's program, it has this little cartoon dinosaur on it... but, um, anyway, yeah. I just feel like I'm somehow damaged now. Like... that really competent person who just got promoted? She just isn't really there anymore.
Can you tell me more about what makes you feel like work isn't safe anymore? Is it related to something specific like the new monitor, or is it a general feeling?

No, it's not really the monitor, though I still think it's completely unnecessary for what we do. It's more about... specific things happening. Like the sound of the badge scanner beeping at the main doors. They actually just updated our whole entry system last month because the old scanners kept malfunctioning, and my coworker Dave actually got locked in the parking garage for three hours on a Sunday. He literally had to order a pizza through the chain-link gate while he waited for facilities to come get him! We still laugh about it. 

But, um... where was I? Right, the office. Yeah, if I hear that scanner beep, or if there are heavy footsteps in the hallway, or even if I just get a late-night deployment alert on my phone... I'm suddenly right back in that office. My chest gets incredibly tight, and I just get this image of the guard on the floor. It just cuts right through whatever I’m doing. It's incredibly distracting. Especially with the deployment alerts, because we use this app that lets you customize the notification sounds, but everyone just leaves it on the default loud siren thing. I keep telling my team we should change it to something softer, like a chime, because from a user-experience perspective, jarring noises just increase cortisol for no reason, you know?
Can you tell me more about that image of the guard in the office — have you ever felt like you were reliving a specific event, or is it more of a general feeling of unease?

It's definitely a specific event. Like, I remember hiding under the table in the main conference room. Which, by the way, has these ridiculous floor-to-ceiling glass walls. I mean, who designs a room with all glass when you're supposed to be looking at a projector screen? The glare is absolutely terrible, especially around 3 PM. We actually had to order these custom motorized blinds for it, but the remote for them is always getting lost because people keep taking it out of the room for some reason. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, I remember hiding there, and I remember the police being there eventually, but there’s this total blank section around when they actually came into the conference room and got me out. It's just... gone. It's exactly like a file is corrupted, no matter how hard I try to open it. And I deal with corrupted data all the time at work. Like, just before all this happened, we had a junior dev accidentally truncate a whole production database table because he didn't check his SQL script, and it took me fourteen straight hours to restore it from our cloud backups. I had to drink so much espresso I was literally vibrating by the end of my shift. But with my memory of getting out of that room... there is no backup to restore from. It's just a blank.
Can you tell me more about what happened when you were hiding under the table in the conference room? Were you in danger or did something happen that scared you for your safety?

Well, yeah, I was definitely in danger. It was a break-in. We were doing an overnight deployment, which is standard when we're rolling out a massive system update because you want to minimize downtime for the users. Usually, those nights are actually kind of fun, we order Thai food and play music while the scripts run. My favorite is this place down the street that does an amazing Pad See Ew, though they recently changed their noodles and they're a bit too mushy now, honestly. 

But anyway, yeah, someone broke in during that deployment. That's when I ended up under the table. And, um, this whole thing, the feelings and the blanks and everything... it's been going on since then. Which was about two years and four months ago now. It's wild to think it's been that long. In tech years, two years and four months is like a lifetime. We've gone through three different project management software migrations since then. First Jira, then Asana, and now we're using this obscure open-source thing that our CTO insisted on because he read a blog post about it. It is an absolute nightmare for tracking sprint velocity, let me tell you. I spend half my week just trying to get the burndown charts to render correctly... but, yeah, two years and four months of dealing with this.
Since the break-in, have you had unwanted memories or flashbacks of the event where you felt like you were reliving it?

Yeah, I mean, I kind of mentioned this a minute ago, but it's like... it's not even a choice. I'll just be sitting there, and if I hear a badge scanner beep, or if someone is walking with heavy footsteps down the hall, it just hits me. Or those late-night deployment alerts on my phone. Seriously, I cannot stress enough how terrible the default alert sound is on that app. It's like this piercing, high-pitched wail. I actually submitted a feature request ticket to the developers about it, suggesting they add a library of ambient sounds instead, because user research shows that sudden loud noises disrupt deep work states. I even linked them to a couple of studies on cognitive load, but they just closed the ticket as "Working as Intended." Which is so typical of third-party vendors, honestly. They never listen to actual end-user feedback. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, when those things happen, the scanner or the footsteps or the alert, I am just suddenly right back in that office. My chest gets incredibly tight, and I get this flash... this image of the guard on the floor. It just completely cuts right through whatever I'm doing. It doesn't matter if I'm in the middle of writing a really complex query or just eating lunch, it just takes over.

latest_inference.note: The patient described recurrent and distressing recollections of a traumatic event (the break-in at work), flashbacks where they feel as though they are reliving the event, and significant distress when exposed to reminders (e.g., badge scanner beeps, footsteps, deployment alerts). They also described avoidance behaviors and memory gaps related to the trauma. These symptoms align with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, unspecified, F43.10. Other candidates (e.g., depression, anxiety disorders, adjustment disorder) are less consistent with the specificity and duration of the trauma-related symptoms described.
